consensus_summary: Consensus primary meaning is spiritual/covenantal unfaithfulness (idolatry and apostasy as marital infidelity) by a people or system bound to God; the Revelation 17–18 harlot is a corrupt religious-political-economic power whose concrete referent is disputed (Rome dominant, also apostate church, Jerusalem, or world system).
book_summary: A covenant city or people unfaithful to its Husband while keeping outward covenant form; in Revelation the Harlot is the great city ruling kings, spiritually Sodom/Egypt/Babylon, literally Jerusalem where Jesus and the prophets were killed (opposite: Virgin).
consensus_core_identification: Harlotry = covenant unfaithfulness/idolatry (inverse of the divine marriage), applied to God’s people or a corrupt system; Rev harlot’s specific ID left open.
book_core_identification: Unfaithful covenant city/people retaining outward form; Rev Harlot = literally Jerusalem.
boundary_disagreement: Book fixes the Revelation harlot as Jerusalem and rejects the commonly taught Rome/apostate world-system readings that consensus lists as dominant or common; consensus treats Jerusalem only as a minority alternative and does not settle the referent.
material_contradiction: None on the shared core (covenant unfaithfulness of a city/people); contradiction is limited to which historical referent the Rev figure is (Jerusalem vs Rome/common alternatives).
rationale: Both center on the same prophetic metaphor (Hosea/Ezekiel-style covenantal adultery of a city/people). The book keeps that category, adds the ‘outward form retained’ condition, and narrows the debated Rev extension to Jerusalem alone—refining boundary/precision rather than replacing the central symbolic identification. Consensus already admits Jerusalem as a minority preterist option, so the book selects and hardens a subset rather than inventing a new core or fully contradicting the primary meaning.
strongest_objection: Rev 17:9 (seven mountains) and 17:18 (city ruling the kings of the earth) plus commercial/imperial detail are standardly read as Rome, not first-century Jerusalem under Roman rule.
